newsitem.title: USA: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS--prices soften, look to supply.
newsitem.headline: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS--prices soften, look to supply.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond prices were quoted down from one-eighth to three-eighths of a point late Monday in cautious trade as players set up for a spate of new offerings this week and responded to softer Treasuries.

"Everyone wants to sit on their hands if they have money," a trader said, explaining that a large number of market participants were hanging onto their cash so that they could buy some of the approximately $3.5 billion of new issues scheduled to be sold this week.

New bonds frequently are considered to offer buyers better structures than they can find in the secondary market, and this week's volume marks a substantial recovery from last week's nearly $2 billion of offerings. But traders said activity was light as many of these sales are scheduled for later this week.

Municipal bond sales on Tuesday will total about $933 million, which breaks down into 12 negotiated sales that add up to $562 million. The largest is a $250 million San Diego Public Facilities Financing Authority sale.
Of the 23 competitive sales, which are worth $371 million, the biggest is a Dade County, Florida, School District's sale of $140 million of general obligation bonds.
Further, the market was wary of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress on Wednesday.
The House Banking Committee postponned the second leg of Greenspan's testimony to March 5 from Thursday as the date conflicted with a joint session of Congress.
Financial markets in the past have reacted with pronounced volatility to Greenspan's comments.

Traders noted that New York issuers are a key feature this week, with the New York Thruway Authority selling nearly $260 million of revenue bonds, while the Municipal Assistance Corp for New York City will sell almost $490 million of bonds on Wednesday.

The Thruway bonds might attract more interest than the MAC issue, in part due to the issue's attractive credit rating and in part due to its structure, which is expected to include long maturities, a trader suggested.
"MAC always seems to pique people's interest though I think Thruway's will be more of a focus," he said, noting the longest bond MAC planned to sell in its refunding was 2008.
The top yield for the issues in the 2008 maturity was 4.875 percent.

Another factor making trading difficult was the continuing absence of retail investors, who still appeared to be more interested in the possibility of getting bigger gains in equities, a picture that has not changed for the past six to 12 months or so. And traders noted that municipal issues are priced fairly richly when compared to Treasuries.

"We're at a pretty steamy numbers, without a tremendous amount of retail because they are still looking at the stock market. You have to be pretty careful about taking out and putting on positions," a trader said.

March U.S. Treasury bonds lost 10 ticks to 112-20/32, while March municipal bond futures shed six ticks to 116-30/32. The spread between the two futures contracts, both traded on the Chicago Board of Trade, stood at plus 138 ticks.

In the secondary market, actively traded issues included Denver Colorado City and County Airport Revenues of November 2025, which have a 5-1/2 percent coupon, and were bid at 5.74 percent, NET, up one basis point.
And Houston, Texas, Water and Sewer System Revenues of December 2025, which pay a 5-1/4 percent coupon, were bid at 5.63 percnet, NET, a gain of one basis point.
